title: The Alpha 21264 Microprocessor
decision: Pursued absolute performance leadership by combining aggressive clock speed (500–600 MHz in 0.35 µm, six-metal CMOS) WITH advanced microarchitectural techniques (out-of-order, speculative execution, deep buffering), rather than trading one for the other.
alternatives_or_rejected: Implicitly rejected the prior-Alpha strategy of relying primarily on clock speed advantage with simpler in-order pipelines (as in 21164). The paper states early analysis showed more aggressive micro-architectural techniques were possible while continuing leadership clock frequencies.
rationale: Absolute performance leadership was again a project goal; detailed architectural and circuit analysis in early stages showed that more aggressive micro-architectural techniques were possible while continuing the leadership clock frequencies that have become an Alpha tradition.
outcome: 30+ SPECint95 and 58+ SPECfp95; 15 M transistors; 2.2 V; 3.1 cm²; 587-pin PGA; up to 2.4 BIPS.

title: The Alpha 21264 Microprocessor
decision: Fetch and execute up to four instructions per cycle with out-of-order and speculative execution, adding a 'map' stage for register renaming to the 21164-like 7-stage pipeline.
alternatives_or_rejected: The 21164 predecessor was in-order; the 21264 design team chose to add out-of-order and speculative execution. The paper frames the map stage as 'one notable addition' fundamental to the 21264's out-of-order techniques.
rationale: Out-of-order execution lets instructions execute as soon as possible and in parallel with other non-dependent work, which results in faster execution because critical-path computations start and complete quickly. Speculative execution maximizes performance by fetching/executing down predicted paths.
outcome: With more functional units and dynamic execution, the 21264 is 50–200% faster than the 21164 for many applications, even though both fetch at most four instructions per cycle.

title: The Alpha 21264 Microprocessor
decision: Implemented a 64 KB, 2-way set-associative instruction cache (vs. the 8 KB direct-mapped I-cache of the 21164), and added line prediction and way prediction to keep the fetch pipe full.
alternatives_or_rejected: Rejected continuing with the 21164's 8 KB direct-mapped I-cache. The paper states the 64 KB 2-way I-cache 'offers much improved hit rates as compared to the 8K direct-mapped instruction cache used in the Alpha 21164.'
rationale: A larger, 2-way I-cache improves hit rates; line/way prediction provides the fast access times of a direct-mapped cache and eliminates bubbles in non-sequential control flows, enabling 4 instructions/cycle delivery to the out-of-order engine.
outcome: The instruction fetcher speculatively fetches through up to 20 branch predictions to supply a continuous instruction stream; the 21264 can fetch four instructions per cycle at 500–600 MHz. (Detailed branch-predictor sub-structure is described in secondary sources based on this paper.)

title: The Alpha 21264 Microprocessor
where_in_paper: Map stage / Register renaming (Section 3, per secondary detailing)
decision: Performed register renaming by mapping each instruction's result to one of 80 physical registers (40 integer + 40 floating point), assigning a unique 8-bit 'inum' and loading instructions into a reorder buffer and collapsible issue queues.
alternatives_or_rejected: Not explicitly contrasted in the paper text we have; however the design clearly chose a merged rename + architectural register file approach (physical register holds results before and after commit, no separate architectural register file, no data copying on commit) over alternatives like a separate architectural register file.
rationale: Renaming exposes instruction-level parallelism — the map stage is described as 'fundamental to the 21264's out-of-order techniques.' The rename table is designed not to stall as long as at least eight free physical register names are available.
outcome: Supports 80 instructions in flight; enables out-of-order issue of up to six instructions per cycle (four integer + two floating-point) from 20-entry integer and 15-entry floating-point issue queues. (Subclustering of integer queues and the one-cycle inter-cluster bypass penalty are detailed in secondary sources derived from this paper.)

title: The Alpha 21264 Microprocessor
decision: Built a high-bandwidth memory system: separate 64 KB 2-way L1 I/D caches with non-blocking, speculative load/store ordering, 32 outstanding loads and 32 outstanding stores, an 8-entry victim buffer, and an off-chip L2 cache.
alternatives_or_rejected: The paper emphasizes that 'the 21264 can service many parallel memory references to all caches in the hierarchy, as well as to the off-chip memory system' — implicitly rejecting a narrow, in-order memory pipe. L2 was moved off-chip vs. prior generations.
rationale: A high-bandwidth memory system can quickly deliver data values to the execution core, providing robust performance for a wide range of applications, including those without cache locality. This permits very high bandwidth data access.
outcome: The processor sustains more than 1.3 GBytes/sec on the Stream benchmark; many parallel memory references allow very high bandwidth data access even for applications without cache locality.
